When writer and musician Samantha Shokin noticed her cover of a public domain Bulgarian folk song had been copyright struck on YouTube, she assumed it would be easy to fix. It wasn’t. And trying to figure out what happened led her to discover an AI content mill that is running 500 slop-filled channels and abusing YouTube’s automated copyright detectors.

“Any human would agree with me that there’s something clearly wrong here that needs to be fixed, but I can’t get in touch with a human being,” Shokin said.

Shokin’s journey is a modern nightmare that highlights the ways AI can be weaponized against human creators, and the ways people fall through the cracks of big tech’s automated systems.

During the pandemic, Shokin recorded a 50 second version of the Bulgarian folk song ‘Bre Petrunko’ and uploaded it to SoundCloud , where it didn’t get much traction. Two years later, she uploaded it to YouTube and watched as her cover grew in popularity, gaining 125,000 views in four years.

Last summer, she noticed an uptick in comments on the video. Unbeknownst to Shokin, her version of “Bre Petruinko” had become popular among DJs and electronic artists and had been sampled in dozens of songs. Someone in the comments pointed her towards one of the more popular tracks. “ I look up this video and it’s something that has millions of hits [...] and 30 seconds into this track I hear my own voice and I was utterly shocked. I didn’t know how to react,” she said (the video has more than 4 million views).

“The first thing that comes to mind is, ‘Oh my god, someone stole my voice and didn’t credit me,’” she said. Shokin said she talked to a lot of DJs and figured out how they’d gotten her voice. They’d purchased a pack of samples from a company called Loopmasters that was selling her version of “Bre Petruinko” as part of its “Folk Legends” set .

“I got in touch with the distributor and they were deeply apologetic. They were unaware that this had happened and they immediately tried to make right of the situation and granted me royalties on the sample pack,” Shokin said. “At that point, countless DJs and music producers had been using my voice for their own tracks, unbeknownst to me. At least I’m aware and at least I was making something off of it and I was satisfied with that. I didn’t love the way that it came about, but whatever, they tried to make right of the situation.”

But Shokin’s “Bre Petruinko” saga wasn’t over. Last month, she opened YouTube and noticed her original recording was gone. A company called Media Nov Records had issued a copyright strike against her song, and YouTube had taken it down.She thought it would be easy to get this reversed. It’s a public domain folk song and she had the original recordings and a history with a distributor. “If I just explain it to YouTube, they’ll understand,” she thought.

Media Nov Records advertises itself as a “distribution company” that that partners with artists to release their music on digital platforms. But a lot of its website focuses on rights management and copyright protection. “At Media Nov, we go above and beyond to safeguard your musical creations. Our comprehensive rights management system leverages cutting-edge technology and legal expertise to ensure you receive the royalties you deserve,” it said on its website.

YouTube uses automated systems to work through copyright claims. When someone files a claim against a video, the company tends to automatically approve it. The original uploader can file a “counterclaim,” where they argue that the video should stay up, or that it should not be demonetized.

Shokin filed two counterclaims, but neither worked. “It's unclear to us whether you have a valid reason for filing a counter notification, so we won't be able to honor your request,” YouTube said in its last denial. It told her to contact the copyright holder; in this case, it was a public domain song and so there was no actual “copyright holder,” just Media Nov, which was claiming to hold it.

“I tried emailing them,” she said. “I tried calling them. There doesn’t appear to be a working phone line. I got in touch with [Loopmaster, which was selling her recording]. They tried getting in touch. I’m being ignored by everybody, by YouTube, by this media company that, like, the website seems to be entirely AI-generated, and all I want is to talk to a human about this.”

Media Nov’s site boasted about its use of automated DMCA takedowns, YouTube content ID management, and AI-powered content recognition. “Our advanced AI identifies your music across platforms ensuring accurate tracking and protection,” it said. The company says it has been in existence since 1996, but Archive.org ’s Wayback Machine doesn’t show much of a web presence until last year. Its website is basic and barebones.

The company has two addresses on its website. One is an apartment building in Los Angeles on Marina Del Rey. The other is the Black Church in Dublin, Ireland — a cathedral that’s been converted into an office space. The site listed a Los Angeles phone number that was busy every time 404 Media tried to call it.

According to corporate paperwork filed in Ireland and reviewed by 404 Media, Media Nov Records was founded a little more than a year ago. Its listed address is the Black Church in Ireland but both of its shareholders gave addresses in Turkey.

404 Media found four different YouTube pages managed by Media Nov Records. Each contained hundreds of videos — many with AI-generated art assets and music. The songs are sometimes cross posted between the different channels and are mostly looping electronic beats. Think low effort “lofi beats” knock offs. The art assets are footage of sports cars, anime girls, and AI-generated pictures of women. The songs are cross posted on multiple channels and often generate fewer than 100 views. Each also has few YouTube shorts that revolve around “random acts of kindness.” A Douyin (the Chinese version of TikTok) watermark is present in some of these videos.

For example, recent YouTube shorts on its flagship page include a basic beat playing over an AI-generated woman mopping the floor of a store while being berated by her AI-generated boss. Another features an AI-generated woman crying over a well, and a crew of men rescuing her child. One of its other pages looks like this:

Media Nov Records told 404 Media that it operates 500 of these channels and “works with various artists, content creators, and music partners.” The company did not initially return emails or phone calls from Shokin or Loopmaster, but responded to an email from 404 Media.

It said it would look into its copyright claim of Shokin’s track. “We remain willing to review the relevant ownership documentation, original audio files, and supporting evidence to investigate the copyright claim thoroughly. If an error is identified, we are committed to taking appropriate corrective action promptly,” it said.

After 404 Media requested comment, Media Nov Records responded to Shokin and asked her to provide “relevant documentation supporting her ownership of the recording, including original audio files, recording evidence, original publication dates, and any other supporting materials,” which is a wild request considering that it has nothing to do with her recording and does not own the copyright.

The company told 404 Media that Shokin and Loopmaster’s emails had gone to its spam folder. “Regarding ‘Bre Petrunko,’ we would like to clarify that the musical composition and arrangement rights associated with Philip Koutev’s work must be distinguished from the rights in any individual sound recording. Media Nov Records also holds certain rights relating to the relevant musical content,” the company told Shokin in an email reviewed by 404 Media.

“Bre Petrunko” is an old folk song with no known writer. It’s primarily sung and most performances of it do not use instruments. Philip Koutev is a Bulgarian composer who popularized a version of the song in 1963. He died in 1982 and the copyright for that particular version is held by the Smithsonian . There are also many other versions of the song on YouTube , some with millions of views .

“Recording your own cover or performance does not automatically establish ownership of the underlying composition or arrangement. Likewise, rights in the underlying musical work do not automatically establish ownership of your particular recording,” Media Nov said.

“It’s ironic that they’re in the copyright business,” Shokin said. “It’s not the arrangement that’s in question. It’s the voice and performance [...] they clearly have no clue what they’re talking about.”

It's unclear why Media Nov Records brought Koutev into the conversation. 404 Media asked which song or work in its catalog triggered the copyright notice against Shokin but Media Nov Records did not respond.

“That makes it really ridiculous,” Alfred Steiner, an artist and copyright lawyer, told 404 Media . “If it’s her voice and her playing instruments, what could she possibly be infringing if it’s a folk song from the 19th century?”

The situation between Shokin and Media Nov Records sounded odd to Steiner. “I've seen lots of providers where you say ‘I have the rights’ and basically say nothing more than that, and they put it back because they’re taking a risk now. They’re harming her. If they just put it back, they’re at no risk,” he said.

“It sounds, to me, like a small company — despite the fact that they represent or run 500 YouTube channels — that are understaffed and is using a lot of different tools, probably a lot of AI, to identify tracks that are ostensibly owned by its clients and then automatically filing takedown requests,” he said. “They’re probably taking down far more than they have the right to take down.”

Minutes after it sent Shokin an email asking for proof she’d recorded the song, Media Nov Records followed up in an email addressed to both 404 Media and Shokin. “Following our review, Media Nov Records has decided to retract the copyright removal request for Samantha Shokin’s video. We are taking this step because the video has not generated revenue or received views, and we do not consider maintaining the removal request necessary at this stage,” it said. “However, this decision does not constitute a waiver of any rights we may hold. We intend to initiate appropriate legal proceedings regarding the underlying copyright dispute.”

Around 24 hours later, Shokin’s original video was back up. A spokesperson for YouTube confirmed that it reinstated the video after the claimant withdrew their complaint.

“It sounds like they got scared and feel like this is not a battle worth fighting,” Shokin said after seeing the email from Media Nov Records.

“Submitting a takedown request for rights that you don’t have can subject you to liability which includes actual damages and costs and attorney’s fees,” Steiner told 404 Media. “Doing this on a slipshod, shotgun approach is inadvisable from my perspective. Of course, if all of the people you end up offending are small parties and don’t have the resources to respond through the court system, and you are a fly-by-night entity that is hard to pin down and nobody knows who you are [...] it can be difficult to get a remedy.”

Shokin said she felt vindicated but was unhappy that it took a journalist emailing Media Nov Records to get them to listen to her. “They got my emails and they got Loopmaster’s email and they were just ignoring it because they only decided to respond because they got scared that it’ll be bad press,” she said. “It’s just not great all around. The whole system is broken. It feels like a broken system.”

It was a fun few weeks while it lasted. People using both Anthropic’s Claude and OpenAI’s Codex to do AI-powered “reverse-engineering” or decompiling are now hitting guardrails or having their accounts limited while trying to do things like unbrick their internet-of-things devices or remove surveillance ads from their smart TVs.

Several people have reported triggering “safety checks” in Claude Code that prevented them from doing AI-powered reverse engineering; a highly upvoted Reddit post in r/ClaudeCode reads “The Dream is dead. Reverse Engineer Anything (REA) is not likely to work with Claude.” A thread in the Reverse Engineer Anything Discord from last week reads, “Claude is refusing to decompile anything,” with multiple users responding saying they have hit similar walls. And X user log4j, who used OpenAI’s Codex to reverse engineer Samsung TVs, reported having their OpenAI account banned for violating its rules on “cyber abuse.” Other users said they asked Codex to reverse engineer hardware or their own code now say they have either been warned by the company or had their accounts restricted . A project called Decomp.wtf that made it easier to reverse engineer software and games has also shut down in recent days.

As we reported last month, Reverse Engineer-Anything has made it easy for people to use AI tools to hack electronics that they own and replace a manufacturer’s software or operating system with an open source or vibecoded one. People have installed new operating systems on their smart TVs, have turned baby monitors into AI assistants, have unbricked internet-of-things devices that were abandoned by their manufacturers, and have installed new software on very old hardware. At the time, I wasn’t sure how I felt about the trend, but as I’ve seen people take ownership and control back over the devices that manufacturers have purposefully bricked, turned into spyware, or have placed artificial limitations on, I have come to see AI-powered reverse engineering of electronic devices as one of the few LLM uses genuinely worth getting excited about. And so big companies have immediately taken steps to restrict this behavior.

The policy tweaks show that big AI corporations will protect other big corporations when their users find ways to use LLMs to circumvent the artificial constraints that hardware manufacturers put on their devices. AI-powered copyright circumvention is OK with big tech when it’s a massive company scraping the entire internet to build their LLMs, but is not OK when people then use those tools to liberate their internet-of-things devices. It’s not the end of AI-powered reverse engineering, but people suddenly getting locked out of their accounts for asking AI to reverse engineer their gadgets suggests that the future of this practice lies in open weight, local, and uncensored models, making it less accessible to the masses and the people who could probably benefit from it most.

Tarun Gogineni, an OpenAI engineer, tweeted that people are not supposed to have their OpenAI accounts restricted for reverse engineering: “these blocks are mostly accidental and a result of difficult decision boundaries; there is no prohibition against reverse engineering with codex. it’s getting fixed,” he tweeted.

But people who are doing AI-powered reverse-engineering suggest that they are moving away from big companies’ models to alternatives where they aren’t going to have their accounts disabled or have to figure out how to work around AI company guardrails.

“My general experience about reverse-engineering getting blocked has been more or less 100% correlated with the ‘cyber’ category blocks I have received. My take is that the lab[s] are probably under pressure to not have their models take part in some kind of criminal hacking activities and their cyber guardrails are erring on the side of being too strict,” Matt Brown, principal consultant at Brown Fine Security and someone who has been using AI to reverse-engineer devices, told 404 Media. “I am investing in hardware and trying to stay up to speed because the frontier labs guardrails will randomly change without warning on the same model. For my security research and pentesting work I really don’t want to invest tooling and energy into an ecosystem that will eventually lock me out. These guardrails on the frontier side have come at the same time as open weight models from (mostly) China are getting better and better.”

Brown posted a YouTube video last week explaining how he found hidden Bluetooth commands in an internet-of-things gas monitor attached to his propane tank with the open weight model GLM 5.3. He has explained in various posts that the guardrails big companies are putting on reverse engineering are why local AI and open weight models are important.

AI-powered reverse-engineering isn’t going anywhere, but it does look like it’s going to become much harder to use the most popular frontier models from OpenAI and Anthropic for it. It’s unclear how much longer it will be possible for you to open an OpenAI Codex window, ask it to find a smart TV hooked up to your network, and tell it to install a new operating system on it. Moving forward, it looks like this type of work will be best done with open source, open weight, uncensored, and local models. That’s a bummer, because one of the things that was so exciting about the Reverse Engineer-Anything trend was how easily accessible it had become.

Last month, researchers and law professors at Cornell Tech, Columbia University, and New York University published a paper about how cheap, AI-assisted reverse-engineering is challenging big manufacturers’ dominance over the devices their make, and is challenging existing intellectual property law.

“AI systems can identify hardware components, extract firmware, decompile object code, and clone entire apps. The resulting struggle between technology vendors and reverse engineers will challenge a wide range of laws, including trade secret, copyright, anti-circumvention, computer misuse, and contract,” they write. “The law of reverse engineering was built for a world where opening a device took time, tools, and rare expertise. That friction is vanishing as agents whittle endless, precise picks for the many little locks that fill our digital lives.”

In recent days, people have started modifying older digital cameras with new, vibe-coded operating systems. In a video about hacking old cameras, the YouTuber Breno Loves Cameras explains why it’s such a big deal and why camera companies don’t like it; that same logic can be applied to any device manufacturer.

“Camera companies have this practice of keeping features to release on newer cameras, and having distinctions [in features] in camera lines,” the YouTuber Breno said in one video. “This is breaking that from those big companies, which are going to lose a lot of money if this becomes a big thing.”

Through that lens, it’s easy to see why big companies are protecting other big companies. People finally found a thing to do with AI tools that gives consumers a bit more control over the devices they bought; it must be immediately stamped out.

“This vibe-code hacking is only called ‘reverse’ when somebody who lacks a trillion dollars is doing it,” the science fiction author Bruce Sterling tweeted. “When you ‘reverse engineer’ the entire Internet Common Crawl, you just built a nice AI model.”

World of Warcraft: Forever, a re-imaginging of the legendary MMO, comes out Wednesday. The idea is to recapture the feeling of discovery and wonder players had when adventuring across its world for the first time back in 2004.

But 2026 is a very different time. Subreddits dedicated to the game are already overrun with AI-generated addons that rip off longtime developers’ work, and a company that helps players track their damage output tells me it is making changes to its API because of the inundation of AI slop addons.

Warcraft Logs is a long-running site made by Archon.gg that lets players track and share their logs of particular in-game fights so they can analyze them for ways to get better. This works by players downloading Archon’s software which records the data of their fights and uploads them to the site. Warcraft Logs makes its API available for free to other developers. It used to be mostly hobby developers, the CEO of Archon.gg and Warcraft Logs, who goes by Sildri Silentcrest, told me. Now, it’s increasingly commercial projects, which are supposed to ask for permission in order to head off projects that would break Warcraft Logs’ terms of service or wouldn’t be able to scale.

“There’s been [an] explosion of development,” Silentcrest said. “Now, we’re averaging a[t] least one commercial ask per day. And I’m sure there are more that are commercializing without our approval. One new World of Warcraft analysis company every day! It's hard to keep up.”

At the root of many of these is the explosion of vibe-coded sites and addons. Addons are custom pieces of software a World of Warcraft player loads into their game for a specific benefit. Maybe they want a guide on the most optimal questing path to take, so an addon shows them the way on their minimap; or they want to make big changes to the UI. Some developers make real money from these, either by running Patreons or receiving ad revenue from Curseforge, the main repository for World of Warcraft addons.

If you scrolled any of the World of Warcraft subreddits in the past few weeks, you likely came across someone posting about the new addon they ‘created’. Sometimes the poster discloses they used AI, other times they add an update later after being called out. There’s even a tool for players to use Claude or Codex while they’re in World of Warcraft, so they can keep making addons in the game.

And with the flood, Warcraft Logs is changing its own API. “We're changing our API to better align with the applications we want to enable. We like things that help our community to dive deeper into their data, like tools that give you a deep dive on why you died to a boss or how you can improve on your next attempt. We don’t like things that effectively scrape lots of the data from our site to show surface-level info on their own site. Unfortunately, the ‘scrape and show basic statistics’ type has become much more prevalent,” Silentcrest said. They said Warcraft Logs is also introducing a paid commercial key “so that developers with commercial ambitions can support the foundation for the projects.”

Addons have been a crucial and thriving part of World of Warcraft for essentially the game’s entire life. Developers have spent many, many hours crafting those over the years. Now, AI is ripping those off too.

“People are making rip-offs of my work and copying my ideas,” plusmouse, a well-known addon creator , told me. Plusmouse gave one example: a particular design for nameplates in the game, which are the bars that appear above an enemy’s head.

“Prior to that releasing I hadn’t seen any addons adopt that style of design, and now, it feels like every AI addon ends up using that idea,” they said. Plusmouse has found in some cases the code is so similar in the AI-generated versions, that they submit copyright complaints to Curseforge. “Sometimes the code is so similar the complaint results in a takedown, other times it’s just different enough to get away with it, despite feeling like my solution. Borrowing ideas is normal in addon development, but doing it on the scale that AI permits isn’t,” they said. Plusmouse said they made some of their GitHub repositories private, which they believe has stopped LLMs from using their code.

Another key part of World of Warcraft: Forever is that the game is letting players engage with it in their own, preferred way.

“If I can be hopeful, the ubiquity of services under development will allow people to pick their own experience,” Silvercrest added. “If they want to take their time and explore in a relaxed manner, then they can. If they have limited time and want to get to endgame content quickly, they can do that too. On the flip side, my worry is that there will be lots of abandonware that will frustrate users with out-of-date information, buggy software, and vulnerabilities.”

Silvercrest said staff at Warcraft Logs “feel pressure to do more,” and the site has used some AI itself for research and some code review. “We have a small team. People are using our API to vibecode features that are on our own to do list. Should we take those features off our list? Or should we bite the bullet and lean into AI tools ourselves?”

They added, “Two years ago, say we had 200 developers using our API and two or three or four were being abusive. Today, 10,000 developers are using our API and 1,000 are being abusive. The ratio has changed, and that really feels bad. It used [to] be developers respecting other developers’ hard work. I'm not sure what’s changed. Is it that Claude doesn’t read the ToS? Or is it that the new developers don’t care as much as the old? We seriously love some of the tools that this coding accessibility has enabled, but policing API use has become a struggle.”
